Data Selection for ERMs

Steve Hanneke Email: steve.hanneke@gmail.com Affiliation:     Shay Moran Email: smoran@technion.ac.il Affiliation:     Alexander Shlimovich Email: ashlimovich@campus.technion.ac.il Affiliation:     Amir Yehudayoff Email: yehudayoff@technion.ac.il Affiliation: 
Abstract

Learning theory has traditionally followed a model-centric approach, focusing on designing optimal algorithms for a fixed natural learning task (e.g., linear classification or regression). In this paper, we adopt a complementary data-centric perspective, whereby we fix a natural learning rule and focus on optimizing the training data. Specifically, we study the following question: given a learning rule 𝒜\mathcal{A} and a data selection budget nn, how well can 𝒜\mathcal{A} perform when trained on at most nn data points selected from a population of NN points? We investigate when it is possible to select n≪Nn\ll N points and achieve performance comparable to training on the entire population.

We address this question across a variety of empirical risk minimizers. Our results include optimal data-selection bounds for mean estimation, linear classification, and linear regression. Additionally, we establish two general results: a taxonomy of error rates in binary classification and in stochastic convex optimization. Finally, we propose several open questions and directions for future research.

keywords
Data Selection, Empirical Risk Minimizers, Compression Schemes, Machine Teaching, Active Learning.

1 Introduction

Roughly speaking, machine learning stands on two legs: (i) Data and (ii) Training algorithms. While much of the research and development in machine learning has focused on improving training algorithms – through advanced architectures, optimization techniques, and novel learning paradigms – the selection and quality of data also play a crucial role. Recognizing this, Andrew Ng has championed a data-centric approach to AI, emphasizing the critical role of high-quality data in machine learning systems (Press, 2021). He contrasts model-centric methodologies, which focus on improving algorithms to handle noisy or imperfect data, with data-centric methodologies, which prioritize enhancing the quality and representativeness of the data itself while holding the algorithm fixed.

Historically, learning theory has predominantly adopted a model-centric perspective, focusing on understanding and improving training algorithms. A common approach is to fix the learning task—often modeled by a hypothesis class—and then study or design optimal algorithms tailored to that task. This framework, grounded in simplifying assumptions such as independent and identically distributed (IID) samples or realizability within a hypothesis class, provides clarity and mathematical rigor for algorithmic design. However, these assumptions often overlook the intricacies of data selection, leaving this crucial aspect largely unexplored.

Our study focuses on the following basic theoretical problem, inspired by the data-centric perspective: given a large batch of NN data points (representing the population), how can we select a subset of nn examples (n≪Nn\ll N) such that training a fixed, natural training algorithm – say, an Empirical Risk Minimizer (ERM) with respect to a natural loss – exclusively on these nn examples yields a model whose performance, in terms of loss, is nearly as good as a model trained on the entire population? This question is a basic example of a data-centric problem, aligning with the growing recognition of the importance of data quality in machine learning.

Overarching Question

Given a natural learning rule 𝒜\mathcal{A} and a data selection-budget nn, how well can 𝒜\mathcal{A} perform when trained on at most nn data points from the population?

This question is also motivated by other perspectives. Computationally, it relates to preprocessing techniques to select a small subset of the training set, thereby simplifying the training process and reducing computational overhead. Statistically, it connects to deriving generalization bounds through sample compression arguments.

1.1 Warmup: Mean Estimation

As a basic case study, consider the following simple regression task: suppose we have a dataset D={z1,…,zN}⊆ℝD=\{z_{1},\ldots,z_{N}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}, where DD is treated as a multiset (i.e., the order does not matter, but repetitions are allowed). The goal is to output a point h∈ℝh\in\mathbb{R} that minimizes the squared loss:

LD​(h)=1N​∑zi∈D(h−zi)2.L_{D}(h)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{z_{i}\in D}(h-z_{i})^{2}.

A simple calculation shows that the minimizer h⋆=h⋆​(D)h^{\star}=h^{\star}(D) is the mean h⋆=1N​∑izih^{\star}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i}z_{i}. Accordingly, we consider the natural learning rule which, when given a sequence of numbers z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n}, outputs their average 1n​∑izi\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}z_{i}.

Our question becomes: can we select a small subdataset of points from the dataset DD such that applying the algorithm to this subdataset yields a guarantee close to the optimum value? More formally, given a dataset DD and a selection budget n≥1n\geq 1, we want to investigate how closely we can approximate LD⋆=minh∈ℝ⁡LD​(h)=LD​(h⋆)L_{D}^{\star}=\min_{h\in\mathbb{R}}L_{D}(h)=L_{D}(h^{\star}). Let

LD⋆​(n)=minz1,…,zn∈D⁡LD​(1n​∑izi).L_{D}^{\star}(n)=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\in D\end{subarray}}L_{D}\Biggl(\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}z_{i}\Biggr).

Thus, LD⋆​(n)L_{D}^{\star}(n) measures the performance when selecting the best possible nn points for training. Note that LD⋆​(N)=LD⋆L_{D}^{\star}(N)=L_{D}^{\star}.

In the following theorem, we quantitatively characterize the optimal multiplicative approximation factor between LD⋆​(n)L_{D}^{\star}(n) and LD⋆L_{D}^{\star}, for any selection budget nn.

Theorem 1 (Mean Estimation).
For every n≥1n\geq 1, supD⊆ℝLD⋆​(n)LD⋆=2​n2​n−1,\sup_{D\subseteq\mathbb{R}}\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(n)}{L_{D}^{\star}}=\frac{2n}{2n-1}, where DD ranges over all finite multisets of ℝ\mathbb{R}. Above, the ratio LD⋆​(n)LD⋆\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(n)}{L^{\star}_{D}} is defined to be 11 when LD⋆​(n)=LD⋆=0L_{D}^{\star}(n)=L_{D}^{\star}=0. If only LD⋆=0L_{D}^{\star}=0, the ratio is defined as ∞\infty.

This result provides a worst-case guarantee: for any dataset DD, there exists a selection of nn points whose average achieves a loss at most (1+12​n−1)\left(1+\frac{1}{2n-1}\right) times the optimal loss, and no better guarantee is possible in general. It is likely that this bound can be improved in specific cases of interest—such as when the mean is one of the data points or when a data point is very close to the mean.

The above result is stated in terms of multiplicative approximation guarantees rather than additive ones. Multiplicative guarantees are natural in this setting, as they remain invariant under scaling, whereas additive guarantees are less meaningful due to the unbounded nature of the loss.

Proof Sketch.

The lower bound is achieved by a dataset DD consisting of 2​n−12n-1 copies of 00 and one copy of 11, yielding LD⋆​(n)LD⋆=2​n2​n−1\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(n)}{L_{D}^{\star}}=\frac{2n}{2n-1}. The analysis reduces to a simple calculation; see Section B.2 for details.

The upper bound is the more technically challenging part of the proof. It builds on the following generalized version of Carathéodory’s Theorem, which simplifies the analysis of LD⋆​(n)L_{D}^{\star}(n) by reducing it to the case where DD is supported on just two points. The result is stated for general dimension dd and is used here for d=1d=1, but later it will also be applied to higher dimensions (d>1d>1). We use the following notation: let f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} be real functions defined on the same domain. Define 𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(f1,…,fn)\mathtt{conv}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) to be the set of all functions gg such that g=∑αi​fig=\sum\alpha_{i}f_{i}, where αi≥0\alpha_{i}\geq 0 and ∑αi=1\sum\alpha_{i}=1.

Proposition 2 (Carathéodory’s Theorem for Convex Functions).

Let K⊆ℝdK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be convex and closed, and let f1,…,fn:K→ℝf_{1},\dots,f_{n}:K\to\mathbb{R} be strictly convex functions. Then, for any g∈𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(f1,…,fn)g\in\mathtt{conv}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}), there exist indices i1≤…≤id+1i_{1}\leq\ldots\leq i_{d+1} and a function g′∈𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(fi1,…,fid+1)g^{\prime}\in\mathtt{conv}(f_{i_{1}},\dots,f_{i_{d+1}}) such that:

  1. 1.

    arg⁡minx∈K​g′​(x)=arg⁡minx∈K⁡g⁡(x)\arg\min_{x\in K}g^{\prime}(x)=\arg\min_{x\in K}g(x), and

  2. 2.

    minx∈K⁡g′​(x)≤minx∈K⁡g⁡(x)\min_{x\in K}g^{\prime}(x)\leq\min_{x\in K}g(x).

The classical Carathéodory’s Theorem asserts that if x,x1,…,xn∈ℝdx,x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and x∈𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(x1,…,xn)x\in\mathtt{conv}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}), then there exist indices i1≤…≤id+1i_{1}\leq\ldots\leq i_{d+1} such that x∈𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(xi1,…,xid+1)x\in\mathtt{conv}(x_{i_{1}},\ldots,x_{i_{d+1}}). This result can be derived as a special case of Proposition 2 by choosing fi​(x)=‖x−xi‖22f_{i}(x)=\|x-x_{i}\|_{2}^{2},(noting that the function ∑αi​fi​(x)\sum\alpha_{i}f_{i}(x) is minimized when x=∑αi​xix=\sum\alpha_{i}x_{i}). Furthermore, the additional guarantee provided by Item 2 of Proposition 2 instantiates in this setting as follows: in the language of probability theory, the classical Carathéodory asserts that for every finitely supported random variable XX in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, there exists a random variable YY, supported on at most d+1d+1 points from the support of XX, such that 𝔼⁡[X]=𝔼⁡[Y]\mathbb{E}[X]=\mathbb{E}[Y]. Proposition 2 extends this result by guaranteeing that the variance satisfies 𝚅𝚊𝚛⁡(Y)≤𝚅𝚊𝚛⁡(X)\mathtt{Var}(Y)\leq\mathtt{Var}(X). The proof of Proposition 2 follows a similar inductive sparsification process for the convex combination as in the classical Carathéodory Theorem (See (Matoušek, 2002, Theorem 1.2.3, p. 6), originally from (Carathéodory, 1907).) . The key difference is the need for a more careful selection during sparsification to ensure the second item (the inequality between the minimum values) is preserved.

Using Proposition 2, the proof of Theorem 1 proceeds as follows. The loss LD⋆L_{D}^{\star} as a function of xx is a convex combination of NN strictly convex functions, fi​(x)=(x−zi)2f_{i}(x)=(x-z_{i})^{2}. We use Proposition 2 to argue that it suffices to consider datasets DD supported on two points, z1z_{1} and z2z_{2}. An explicit analysis of this case reveals that the largest possible ratio occurs when DD contains 2​n−12n-1 copies of z1z_{1} and 1 copy of z2z_{2}. An elementary calculation then yields the stated bound. The complete proofs of Theorem 1 and Proposition 2 are provided in Section B.

Organization

We study questions of data selection in two main contexts: classification and stochastic convex optimization, with a particular focus on linear classification and linear regression.

The remainder of this manuscript is organized as follows. Section 2 focuses on classification, presenting two main results: one for the class of linear classifiers (Section 2.1) and another that provides a taxonomy for general hypothesis classes (Section 2.1.1). Section 3 parallels this structure in the context of regression, covering results for linear regression (Section 4) and stochastic convex optimization (Section 4.1). Section 5 discusses open problems and potential directions for future research. Related work is discussed throughout the paper, with a more comprehensive review provided in Section A. To enhance readability, we include proof sketches and overviews alongside the main results, while full proofs appear in the appendix (Section B).

2 Classification

2.1 Linear Classification

We begin by considering the class of linear classifiers in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. A dd-dimensional linear classifier (or halfspace) is a function of the form x↦𝚜𝚒𝚐𝚗⁡(w⁡(x)+b)x\mapsto\mathtt{sign}(w(x)+b), where w:ℝd→ℝw:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is a linear functional, and b∈ℝb\in\mathbb{R} is a bias term. Let ℋd\mathcal{H}_{d} denote the class of dd-dimensional linear classifiers. This class is arguably the most studied class in learning theory, and there is a rich variety of learning algorithms that have been developed for it.

In this section, we consider the realizable setting, meaning that the dataset D={(xi,yi)}i=1ND=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N} is consistent with a linear classifier h∈ℋdh\in\mathcal{H}_{d}; that is, h⁡(xi)=yih(x_{i})=y_{i} for all i≤Ni\leq N. We focus on natural ERMs, such as the one that maximizes the margin: a halfspace hh where the separating hyperplane has maximal distance from the training set. For convenience, we refer to this as the max-margin algorithm. More generally, we focus on continuous ERMs, which we now formalize.

In the following definition, we rely on two key notions: (i) a proper algorithm, which is an algorithm whose output classifier always belongs to the hypothesis class (in the context of linear classifiers, this means that the algorithm always outputs a linear classifier), and (ii) for a label sequence y¯=(y1,…,yn)∈{±1}n\bar{y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\in\{\pm 1\}^{n} the set Ry¯R_{\bar{y}} which captures all realizable datasets whose label sequence is y¯\bar{y}:

Ry¯={(x1,…,xn):{(xi,yi)}i=1n​ is realizable by ​ℋd}.R_{\bar{y}}=\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}):\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}\text{ is realizable by }\mathcal{H}_{d}\}.

Note that, as a topological subspace of (ℝd)n(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{n}, the set Ry¯R_{\bar{y}} is open.11 1 This follows because {(xi,yi)}i=1n\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} is realizable if and only if 𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡{xi:yi=+1}\mathtt{conv}\{x_{i}:y_{i}=+1\} and 𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡{xi:yi=−1}\mathtt{conv}\{x_{i}:y_{i}=-1\} are disjoint. Since the convex hulls are compact sets, they are disjoint if and only if the distance between them is strictly positive. By the continuity of the distance function, there exists an open neighborhood UU around (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) such that 𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡{xi′:yi=+1}\mathtt{conv}\{x^{\prime}_{i}:y_{i}=+1\} and 𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡{xi′:yi=−1}\mathtt{conv}\{x^{\prime}_{i}:y_{i}=-1\} are disjoint for all (x1′,…,xn′)∈U(x^{\prime}_{1},\ldots,x^{\prime}_{n})\in U, and hence {(xi′,yi)}i=1n\{(x^{\prime}_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} is realizable.

Definition 3.

We say that a proper algorithm AA is continuous if, for every y¯∈{±1}n\bar{y}\in\{\pm 1\}^{n}, the map F:Ry¯→ℝd+1F:R_{\bar{y}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d+1}, which takes as input (x1,…,xn)∈Ry¯(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in R_{\bar{y}} and outputs the parameters (w,b)∈ℝd+1(w,b)\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1} of the linear classifier A⁡((xi,yi)i=1n)A((x_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}), is continuous.22 2 Linear classifiers admit multiple parameterizations. To ensure uniqueness, we adopt a canonical parameterization by normalizing ww so that its ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm is 1. In the case when w=0w=0 we normalize by setting |b|=1\lvert b\rvert=1.

Thus, an ERM is continuous if the parameters of the linear classifier it outputs are a continuous function of its input. Many practical and well-known algorithms are continuous, for example, those that reduce via a surrogate loss to continuous optimization (e.g., gradient-based algorithms). In particular, the max-margin algorithm, as mentioned above, is continuous.

In this setting, our question becomes: given a realizable dataset D={zi}i=1ND=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N}, where each zi=(xi,yi)z_{i}=(x_{i},y_{i}) is a labeled example, a selection budget nn, and a natural learning rule AA (such as the max-margin algorithm or any other continuous ERM), what is the minimum classification loss that can be achieved by training AA on just nn points from DD?

More formally, for a classifier h:ℝd→{±1}h:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\{\pm 1\}, let the classification loss be defined as:

LD(h)=1N∑i=1N1[h(xi)≠yi],L_{D}(h)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}1[h(x_{i})\neq y_{i}],

where 1​[⋅]1[\cdot] is the indicator function. We aim to study the quantity:

LD⋆​(n,A)=minz1,…,zn∈D⁡LD​(A⁡(z1,…,zn)).L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)=\min_{z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\in D}L_{D}(A(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})).

Here, LD⋆​(n,A)L^{\star}_{D}(n;A) represents the minimum possible classification loss that AA can achieve on DD when trained on a subdataset of nn examples.

Note that because DD is realizable and AA is an ERM, we have LD⋆​(N,A)=0L^{\star}_{D}(N;A)=0. This is because when given the entire dataset, AA outputs a consistent halfspace that correctly classifies all the examples in DD, resulting in a loss of 00.

We now state the main result for linear classification under the max-margin algorithm and for continuous ERMs.

Theorem 4 (Linear Classification).
Let A⋆A^{\star} denote the max-margin algorithm. Then, supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A⋆)={0if ​n>d,12if ​n≤d,\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }n>d,\\ \frac{1}{2}&\text{if }n\leq d,\end{cases} where DD ranges over all realizable datasets. Furthermore, A⋆A^{\star} is optimal in the sense that for every continuous ERM AA (and even for any continuous proper learner), (∀n≤d):supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A)≥12.(\forall n\leq d):\quad\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)\geq\frac{1}{2}.
Proof Sketch.

The result that LD⋆​(n,A⋆)=0L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})=0 for all n≥d+1n\geq d+1 with the max-margin algorithm is classical and can be found in (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1974); see also Appendix A of Long and Long (2020).

We now give a brief overview of our proof of the second part, which shows that if n≤dn\leq d, it is impossible to achieve error less than 1/21/2 with any continuous proper learner. (Note that error 1/21/2 can be achieved by selecting from only two constant hypotheses: the constant +1+1 and the constant −1-1.33 3 These two constant hypotheses assign the same label to all inputs. On any dataset, at least one of these constant functions has error at most 1/21/2, specifically the one that corresponds to the majority label.) To prove this, we employ the probabilistic method to construct, for any arbitrarily small η>0\eta>0, a (d−1)(d-1)-dimensional dataset D⊆ℝd×{±1}D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\{\pm 1\} with the following properties:

  1. 1.

    Every subset of DD containing at most dd points is realizable by ℋd\mathcal{H}_{d}.

  2. 2.

    Every halfspace h∈ℋdh\in\mathcal{H}_{d} has a classification error on DD of at least 12−η\frac{1}{2}-\eta.

  3. 3.

    Every open neighborhood of DD, when viewed as a point in (ℝd)|D|(\mathbb{R}^{d})^{\lvert D\rvert}, includes a realizable dataset.

Using these properties, and leveraging the continuity of the assumed proper learner, we establish the existence of a realizable dataset in the neighborhood of DD on which its error is at least nearly 12\frac{1}{2}.

The continuity assumption in Theorem 4 is necessary for this result. Figure 1 illustrates a natural ERM AA that is not continuous and achieves LD⋆​(n,A)=0L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)=0 for every n>d−1n>d-1. This figure demonstrates how non-continuous ERMs can exploit discontinuities in decision boundaries to achieve better performance. Exploring general ERMs that are not necessarily continuous is a direction we leave for future work.

2.1.1 General Classes

We now shift our attention to ERMs over general hypothesis classes ℋ⊆{±1}X\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{X}, where ℋ\mathcal{H} denotes the set of candidate classifiers from which the ERM selects one that minimizes the loss. Since we now consider general classes, we also allow for arbitrary ERMs and arbitrary datasets.

Let AA be an ERM over ℋ\mathcal{H}, and let DD be a dataset. We define the minimum regret achievable by AA when trained on a subdataset of nn points from DD as:

𝚁ℋ⋆​(n,A,D)=minz1,…,zn∈D⁡[LD​(A⁡(z1,…,zn))−minh∈ℋ⁡LD​(h)],\mathtt{R}^{\star}_{\mathcal{H}}(n;A,{D})=\min_{z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\in D}\left[L_{D}(A(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}))-\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}L_{D}(h)\right],

where the regret is measured relative to the best hypothesis in ℋ\mathcal{H}. By definition, this quantity satisfies 0≤𝚁ℋ⋆​(n,A,D)≤10\leq\mathtt{R}^{\star}_{\mathcal{H}}(n;A,{D})\leq 1, since AA is an ERM over ℋ\mathcal{H}.

To address our overarching question in this general setting, where there is no universally preferred ERM for general hypothesis classes, we focus on the following quantity, which captures the worst-case regret achievable for arbitrary ERMs over ℋ\mathcal{H}:

𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)=supA,D𝚁ℋ⋆​(n,A),\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)=\sup_{A,D}\mathtt{R}^{\star}_{\mathcal{H}}(n;A),

where the supremum is taken over all ERMs AA over ℋ\mathcal{H} and all (finite) datasets DD.44 4 It is also natural to study the quantity infAsupD𝚁ℋ⋆​(n,A)\inf_{A}\sup_{D}\mathtt{R}^{\star}_{\mathcal{H}}(n;A), which focuses on the best possible ERM. This variant relates to proper sample compression schemes, a long-standing open problem for general VC classes (see Section A for further discussion). The following theorem characterizes the behavior of 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n) by classifying all hypothesis classes into one of three distinct regimes as nn grows:

𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)∈{0,Θ~​(1n),1},\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)\in\Bigl\{0,\tilde{\Theta}\left(\frac{1}{n}\right),1\Bigr\},

for all sufficiently large nn.

Theorem 5 (Binary Classification).
Every hypothesis class ℋ⊆{±1}X\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{X} satisfies exactly one of the following: 1. 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)=1\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)=1, for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. (Trivial Rate) 2. C1n≤𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)≤C2⋅log⁡nn\frac{C_{1}}{n}\leq\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)\leq\frac{C_{2}\cdot\log n}{n}, for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Here C1=C1​(ℋ),C2=C2​(ℋ)C_{1}=C_{1}(\mathcal{H}),C_{2}=C_{2}(\mathcal{H}) are positive constants that depend on ℋ\mathcal{H} (but not on nn). (Linear Rate) 3. 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)=0\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)=0, for all sufficiently large n≥n0​(ℋ)n\geq n_{0}(\mathcal{H}). (Zero Rate)

Each item in the taxonomy is associated with a combinatorial characterization, relating it to classical notions in learning theory:

  • •

    Item 1 (Trivial Rate): Hypothesis classes ℋ\mathcal{H} with unbounded VC dimension (i.e., not PAC learnable).

  • •

    Item 2 (Linear Rate): Hypothesis classes ℋ\mathcal{H} with finite VC dimension but unbounded star number (i.e., PAC learnable but not actively PAC learnable, as characterized in Hanneke and Yang (2015)).

  • •

    Item 3 (Zero Rate): Hypothesis classes ℋ\mathcal{H} with finite star number (i.e., actively PAC learnable).

See Section B.3 for more details and the full proof.

The results in Theorem 5 show that selecting the best examples allows for significantly faster rates compared to those achieved in PAC learning, which relies on random examples. For hypothesis classes with finite VC dimension, the PAC learning rate decreases as 1/n1/\sqrt{n}, where nn is the number of training examples. In contrast, data selection achieves much faster rates: linear in Item 2 and zero after a certain point in Item 3.55 5 In PAC learning, for hypothesis classes with unbounded VC dimension, the error rate is 1/21/2, paralleling Item 1 in the theorem.

Proof Sketch.

The behavior of 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n) is closely connected to the concept of ε\varepsilon-nets, a well-studied notion in combinatorics and geometry. For a family of sets ℱ\mathcal{F} over a domain XX and a distribution PP over XX, an ε\varepsilon-net is a subdset N⊆XN\subseteq X such that N∩F≠∅N\cap F\neq\emptyset for every F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F} with P⁡(F)≥εP(F)\geq\varepsilon.

We show that 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n) is essentially determined by the minimum possible size of ε\varepsilon-nets for a family of sets ℱ=ℱ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{F}=\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{H}) corresponding to ℋ\mathcal{H}. This connection, together with known results on ε\varepsilon-nets, establishes the different cases in Theorem 5.

Theorem 4 vs. Theorem 5.

Theorem 4 applies to the class of dd-dimensional half-spaces, which belongs to the second category (finite VC dimension, infinite star number) whenever d≥2d\geq 2. However, its result aligns with the last category, exhibiting a zero-rate behavior. This discrepancy arises because Theorem 4 considers a specific ERM—the max-margin classifier—while Theorem 5 assumes an arbitrary (worst-case) ERM. This distinction highlights how natural ERMs for structured hypothesis classes can lead to significantly better performance in data selection.

One natural question that remains open is to refine the rates in Item 2. Notice that there is a logarithmic gap between the upper and lower bounds in this case. Using results from the theory of ε\varepsilon-nets, it can be shown that both bounds are tight in the sense that there exist classes for which the upper bound is tight and others for which the lower bound is tight. It remains an open problem to provide a full taxonomy of all possible asymptotic rates of 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n) between 1/n1/n and log⁡(n)/n\log(n)/n. This is essentially equivalent to providing a corresponding taxonomy for the sizes of ε\varepsilon-nets.

3 Stochastic Convex Optimization

We now turn to studying data selection for regression problems. This section presents two results that parallel our findings on classification in the previous section. First, in Section 4, we consider the setting of linear regression. Then, in Section 4.1, we present a general result in the broader framework of stochastic convex optimization (SCO).

Stochastic Convex Optimization.

Stochastic convex optimization (SCO) is a special case of the general learning setting introduced by Vapnik (1998), where the loss functions are convex (Shalev-Shwartz, Shamir, Srebro, and Sridharan, 2009). An SCO problem is defined by a convex hypothesis (or parameter) space 𝒲⊆ℝd\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} and an abstract set of examples 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, where each z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} is associated with a convex loss function ℓz:𝒲→ℝ\ell_{z}:\mathcal{W}\to\mathbb{R}. A learning problem is specified by a distribution DD over 𝒵\mathcal{Z}, and the goal is, given a finite sample z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n}, to compute a hypothesis w∈𝒲w\in\mathcal{W} whose population loss LD​(w)=𝔼z∼D​[ℓz​(w)]L_{D}(w)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim D}[\ell_{z}(w)] is nearly optimal, i.e., close to infw∈𝒲LD​(w)\inf_{w\in\mathcal{W}}L_{D}(w).

Example 6 (Linear Regression).

Linear regression provides a simple example of an SCO problem: the parameter space is 𝒲=ℝd\mathcal{W}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, the example space is ℝd×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}, and each example z=(x,y)z=(x,y), where x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}, is associated with the squared loss ℓz​(w)=(w⋅x−y)2\ell_{z}(w)=(w\cdot x-y)^{2}, where “⋅\cdot” denotes the standard dot product in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}.

More generally, SCO can model a wide range of supervised learning problems with convex loss functions.

Weighted Data Selection.

We consider a fractional (or convex) relaxation of the data selection problem, where the selector is allowed to choose convex combinations of the losses associated with the selected examples. Such weighted relaxations are commonly used in the context of coresets, as further discussed below. Specifically, given a dataset D={zi}i=1ND=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} representing the population, the goal is to select a dataset D′D^{\prime} of n≪Nn\ll N examples zi1,…,zin∈Dz_{i_{1}},\ldots,z_{i_{n}}\in D along with non-negative coefficients α1,…,αn\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}, such that applying the ERM to the weighted loss LD′​(w)=∑j=1nαj​ℓzij​(w)L_{D^{\prime}}(w)=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{j}\ell_{z_{i_{j}}}(w) produces an hypothesis wD′∈𝒲w_{D^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{W} whose population loss LD​(wD′)=1N​∑i=1Nℓzi​(w)D′L_{D}(w_{D^{\prime}})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\ell_{z_{i}}(w)_{D^{\prime}} is nearly optimal, i.e., close to infw∈𝒲LD​(w)\inf_{w\in\mathcal{W}}L_{D}(w).

To formalize this, we define the following:

Definition 7.

Consider an SCO problem with parameter space 𝒲\mathcal{W} and an example space 𝒵\mathcal{Z}. Let DD be a (finite) dataset, and let AA be a learning rule. For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, define:

LD⋆​(n,A)=infz1,…,zn∈D,F∈𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(ℓz1,…,ℓzn)LD​(A⁡(F)).L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)=\inf_{\begin{subarray}{c}z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}\in D,\\ F\in\mathtt{conv}(\ell_{z_{1}},\ldots,\ell_{z_{n}})\end{subarray}}L_{D}(A(F)).

Weighted selection of data, as considered here, is a well-established approach in closely related work, particularly in the study of coresets (Bachem, Lucic, and Krause, 2017; Lucic, Faulkner, Krause, and Feldman, 2018; Feldman, 2020; Feldman, Schmidt, and Sohler, 2020). Coresets are small, weighted subsets of a dataset that preserve key properties of the full data, often enabling efficient optimization and learning while maintaining theoretical guarantees. Many coreset techniques achieve this by assigning weights to selected examples, ensuring that the loss landscape of the subdataset closely approximates that of the entire dataset—an approach closely related to our formulation.

Moreover, this weighted relaxation of data selection aligns well with ERMs for convex optimization, as ERMs naturally operate over weighted objective functions. In fact, the weighted optimization problem induced by this relaxation is of the same type as that which ERM algorithms are designed to solve. The weighted and unweighted optimization problems (corresponding to the original data selection problem) also share similar properties, such as smoothness and Lipschitz continuity.

4 Linear Regression

We now present our results for linear regression (Example 6). In linear regression, there is a unique parameter that minimizes the loss whenever the training dataset S={zi}i=1nS=\{z_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} is full-dimensional, that is, it contains dd examples zij=(xij,yij)z_{i_{j}}=(x_{i_{j}},y_{i_{j}}) such that the xijx_{i_{j}} form a basis of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Thus, all ERMs agree on full-dimensional training datasets. When the training dataset is not full-dimensional, there is a linear subspace of minimizers of nonzero dimension, and the ERM rule needs to break ties. In such cases, we focus on ERMs that break ties continuously, such as the learning rule that outputs the hypothesis with minimal Euclidean norm among all empirical risk minimizers. We refer to this learning rule as min-norm ERM.

What does it formally mean for an ERM to break ties continuously? A natural definition is that the map that takes as input (z1,…,zn)∈(ℝd×ℝ)n(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\in(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R})^{n} and outputs the parameters of A⁡((xi,yi)i=1n)A((x_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}) should itself be continuous. However, as we shall see in the proof of Theorem 9, no ERM satisfies this stringent requirement. To address this, we define continuity in a weaker sense.

Definition 8.

Let n≤dn\leq d, and let En⊆(ℝd×ℝ)nE_{n}\subseteq(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R})^{n} denote the set of all datasets ((x1,y1),…,(xn,yn))((x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(x_{n},y_{n})) such that the xix_{i}’s are linearly independent. We say that a learning rule AA is weakly-continuous if, for every n≤dn\leq d, the map that takes as input ((x1,y1),…,(xn,yn))∈En((x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(x_{n},y_{n}))\in E_{n} and outputs the parameters of A⁡((xi,yi)i=1n)A((x_{i},y_{i})_{i=1}^{n}), is continuous on EnE_{n}.

This definition requires tie-breaking to be continuous only on datasets where the xix_{i}’s are linearly independent. For example, the min-norm ERM satisfies this definition. Similarly, any learning rule that selects an ERM by minimizing a continuous regularization function satisfied the definition.

Although this definition does not fully formalize the intuitive requirement of continuous tie-breaking - because it only requires tie-breaking on linearly independent datasets - it ensures that any continuous tie-breaking rule satisfies the definition. There are, however, tie-breaking rules that are not continuous, but still satisfy this weaker definition. In Section C, we introduce a stricter definition that aligns more precisely with the intuitive requirement. We note that working with the weaker Definition 8 strengthens our theorem, as it broadens the scope of our impossibility result to include any ERM that satisfies this more general and less restrictive definition.

We now state the main result for linear regression.

Theorem 9 (Linear Regression).
Let A⋆A^{\star} denote the min-norm ERM. Then, supDLD⋆​(n,A⋆)LD⋆={1if ​n≥2​d,d+1if ​n=d,∞if ​n<d,\sup_{D}\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})}{L^{\star}_{D}}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }n{\geq 2d},\\ d+1&\text{if }n=d,\\ \infty&\text{if }n<d,\end{cases} where DD ranges over all finite datasets and LD⋆=infw∈𝒲LD​(w)L^{\star}_{D}=\inf_{w\in\mathcal{W}}L_{D}(w) denotes the optimal population loss. Above, the ratio LD⋆​(n,A⋆)LD⋆\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})}{L^{\star}_{D}} is defined to be 11 when both the numerator and denominator are 00. If only the denominator is 00, the ratio is defined as ∞\infty. Furthermore, the lower bound in the case n<dn<d holds for every weakly continuous ERM.

This result differs from Theorem 1 in the Warm-Up section, where we analyzed mean estimation under unweighted data selection and showed that achieving optimal performance with a finite selection budget was impossible. Here, we demonstrate that if weighted data selection is allowed, then optimal performance can be attained using a selection budget of only 2​d2d examples. As in the warm-up example, we again consider multiplicative approximation guarantees rather than additive ones, as they are scale-invariant and mathematically cleaner for unbounded losses. However, it would be interesting to explore the analogous question for additive regret (when the parameter space 𝒲\mathcal{W} and the example space 𝒵\mathcal{Z} are compact); we discuss this further in the future work section.

Theorem 9 parallels Theorem 4, which handled continuous ERMs for linear classification, with a curious difference in the case when n=dn=d: in regression, the case of n=dn=d is distinct in that a non-trivial multiplicative approximation guarantee of d+1d+1 is achievable, unlike classification where no non-trivial guarantee exists.

Proof Sketch.

The first item is similar to our variant of Carathéodory’s Theorem (Proposition 2). However, it does not follow directly since the loss functions ℓz\ell_{z} in linear regression are not strictly convex. To circumvent this, we rely on a related theorem by Steinitz (Matoušek et al., 2003, p.8), originally from Steinitz (1916), which states that given a dd-interior point of the convex hull of nn points, there exists a subset with at most 2​d2d points that also has this point as a dd-interior point. A further subtlety arises when some of the individual loss gradients ∇ℓz\nabla\ell_{z} vanish at the min-norm solution. This case requires a different handling, and while more intricate, it is still possible to match the optimal performance with a selection budget of at most d+d′≤2​dd+d^{\prime}\leq 2d, where d′d^{\prime} denotes the dimension of the subspace spanned by the nonzero gradients.

Item 2 follows from a probabilistic argument based on determinantal point processes by Derezinski and Warmuth (2017). Item 3 follows from a similar approach to that used to establish the parallel statement in Theorem 4, adapted to linear regression and the squared loss.

The above result provides a near-complete taxonomy of the multiplicative approximation guarantees for the min-norm ERM, with the case d<n<2​dd<n<2d remaining open. The result only establishes that the approximation ratio in this range is O⁡(d)O(d), and it would be interesting to determine exact bounds in this regime. Notably, Example 10 demonstrates that for any n<2​dn<2d, the approximation ratio exceeds 1, confirming that perfect approximation is unattainable in this range.

Example 10.

To illustrate the Necessity of n≥2​dn\geq 2d in Theorem 9, we construct an example demonstrating that when n<2​dn<2d, the empirical loss LD⋆​(n,A⋆)L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star}) can exceed the optimal population loss LD⋆L^{\star}_{D}. Let us construct the dataset DD as follows:

D={(ei,2)}i=1d∪{(−ei,1)}i=1d,D=\left\{(e_{i},2)\right\}_{i=1}^{d}\cup\left\{(-e_{i},1)\right\}_{i=1}^{d},

where eie_{i} denotes the standard basis vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Since the feature vectors are the standard basis, the squared loss minimization problem decomposes to dd independent problems, one for each coordinate. The optimal solution is w⋆=(12,12,…,12)∈ℝdw^{\star}=\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\ldots,\frac{1}{2}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and its loss is 94\frac{9}{4}. Since D′D^{\prime} contains fewer than 2​d2d points out of 2​d2d, there exists at least one coordinate i∈{1,2,…,d}i\in\{1,2,\ldots,d\} such that D′D^{\prime} does not include both points (ei,2)(e_{i},2) and (−ei,1)(-e_{i},1). (i) If D′D^{\prime} includes (ei,2)(e_{i},2) but excludes (−ei,1)(-e_{i},1) then w′​(i)=2w^{\prime}(i)=2. Thus, its individual loss on the excluded point (−ei,1)(-e_{i},1) is (−w′​(i)−1)2=(−2−1)2=9\left(-w^{\prime}(i)-1\right)^{2}=(-2-1)^{2}=9 while on (ei,2)(e_{i},2) individual loss is 00, and hence LD​(w′)≥LD​(w⋆)+9+0−9/2d>LD​(w⋆)L_{D}(w^{\prime})\geq L_{D}(w^{\star})+\frac{9+0-9/2}{d}>L_{D}(w^{\star}). The case when D′D^{\prime} includes (−ei,1)(-e_{i},1) but excludes (ei,2)(e_{i},2)) is analyzed similarly. (ii) If D′D^{\prime} excludes both (ei,2)(e_{i},2) and (−ei,1)(-e_{i},1) then LD′​(w)L_{D^{\prime}}(w) does not depend on the ii’th coordinate of ww, hence, by the min-norm property w′​(i)=0w^{\prime}(i)=0 and its individual losses on the excluded points (ei,2)(e_{i},2) and (−ei,1)(-e_{i},1) are respectively (0−2)2=4(0-2)^{2}=4 and (0−1)2=1(0-1)^{2}=1. Thus, LD​(w′)≥LD​(w⋆)+5/2−9/4d>LD​(w⋆)L_{D}(w^{\prime})\geq L_{D}(w^{\star})+\frac{5/2-9/4}{d}>L_{D}(w^{\star}).

4.1 A General Result for Strictly Convex Losses

We now present a general result for stochastic convex optimization (SCO) problems.

Theorem 11 (Stochastic Convex Optimization).
Consider a SCO problem with a parameter space 𝒲⊆ℝd\mathcal{W}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} that is closed and convex. Assume further that each loss function ℓz\ell_{z} for z∈𝒵z\in\mathcal{Z} is strictly convex. Then, for any ERM AA, every dataset DD, and any n>dn>d: LD⋆​(n,A)=LD⋆.L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)=L^{\star}_{D}. Moreover, the strict convexity and n>dn>d assumptions are necessary, as illustrated by Examples 22 and 23) in Appendix B.4.2.

The proof of this theorem follows directly from Proposition 2. This result highlights the benefits of using regularization to induce strict convexity in optimization problems. By ensuring strict convexity, one can perform data selection with as few as n=d+1n=d+1 points, significantly reducing the selection budget. More broadly, regularization stabilizes the optimal solution by guaranteeing that it is determined by at most d+1d+1 examples—similar to the role of support vectors in SVMs.

5 Future Research

This work explored optimal data selection for natural algorithms in the contexts of classification and stochastic convex optimization. In classification, we focused on unweighted data selection, while in stochastic convex optimization, we considered weighted data selection.

Data Selection in Regression.

A natural extension of our study is to explore unweighted data selection for regression problems. For example, our analysis can be adapted to show that the results in Theorem 9 for linear regression in the cases n=dn=d and n<dn<d also hold for unweighted data selection. Studying the case of n>dn>d in the unweighted setting remains an open question. It would also be interesting to study weighted data selection for other ERMs, beyond the min-norm ERM addressed in Theorem 9.

Additionally, the case d<n<2​dd<n<2d is not handled by Theorem 9, and it would be interesting to characterize the approximation guarantees in this regime.

Additive Approximation Guarantees.

In this work, we focused on multiplicative approximation guarantees in the context of stochastic convex optimization, as these are natural for unbounded loss functions. Exploring additive approximation guarantees for compact SCO problems is an interesting direction for future research, particularly to understand how they depend on properties such as Lipschitz continuity, smoothness, strong convexity, and the diameter of the parameter space.

Non-Continuous ERMs in Classification.

A natural direction for future research is to relax the continuity assumption in linear classification. Specifically, is it possible to construct an ERM for linear classification that achieves non-trivial guarantees with n≤dn\leq d? As shown in Figure 1, non-continuous ERMs can leverage discontinuities in decision boundaries in the case n=dn=d.

High-Dimensional Mean Estimation.

The mean estimation problem analyzed in Theorem 1 naturally extends to higher dimensions, formulated as a stochastic convex optimization problem with 𝒲=ℝd\mathcal{W}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, 𝒵=ℝd\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{R}^{d}, and loss functions defined as ℓz​(h)=‖z−h‖2\ell_{z}(h)=\|z-h\|^{2}. An interesting question is how the results of Theorem 1 generalize as the dimension dd increases.

For every dd, the following bounds hold: 2​n2​n−1≤supD⊆ℝdLD⋆​(n)LD⋆≤n+1n\frac{2n}{2n-1}\leq\sup_{D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(n)}{L_{D}^{\star}}\leq\frac{n+1}{n}. The lower bound is tight for d=1d=1 by Theorem 1, while the upper bound becomes tight in the limit as d→∞d\to\infty, i.e., limd→∞supD⊆ℝdLD⋆​(n)LD⋆=n+1n\lim_{d\to\infty}\sup_{D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}}\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(n)}{L_{D}^{\star}}=\frac{n+1}{n}. Proofs of these inequalities, which represent partial results on this problem, will be included in the final version of this draft.

An open question is to determine the exact tight bounds for fixed dimensions d=2,3,…d=2,3,\ldots. Another interesting direction is to study bounds for weighted data selection in this problem.

Appendix A Related Work

While most of learning theory has predominantly followed a model-centric approach, focusing on designing and analyzing algorithms, there are a few subareas that can be viewed as more data-centric. One notable example is the study of sample compression schemes (Littlestone and Warmuth, 1986), which aim to derive generalization bounds for algorithms whose outputs depend on a small subset of selected input examples. Another prominent example is active learning (Cohn, Atlas, and Ladner, 1994; Balcan, Beygelzimer, and Langford, 2006; Hanneke, 2014), where the goal is to achieve effective learning by labeling as few examples as possible. A related variant studied by Dasgupta, Hsu, Poulis, and Zhu (2019) considers a black-box active learning model, where the learner interacts with an oracle that returns hypotheses instead of labels. Similarly, Cicalese, Filho, Laber, and Molinaro (2020) develop an active learning algorithm with improved bounds.

More recently, there has been a line of work in machine teaching and coresets that relates to our problem. A coreset is a small weighted subset of a dataset that approximately preserves some key property (e.g., loss, margin, or clustering cost) of the full dataset. This allows for more efficient computation without significant loss in accuracy. Several works have explored different approaches to constructing coresets. Maalouf, Jubran, and Feldman (2019) propose a new algorithm for computing Carathéodory sets with improved efficiency, reducing the complexity to O⁡(n​d)O(nd). In the context of approximation, Feldman, Schmidt, and Sohler (2020) show that low-rank matrix approximations can estimate distances to compact sets spanned by kk vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} up to a (1+ϵ)(1+\epsilon) factor. Expanding this direction, Maalouf, Eini, Mussay, Feldman, and Osadchy (2024) explore a learning-based approach to constructing coresets, while Tukan, Zhou, Maalouf, Rus, Braverman, and Feldman (2023) and Borsos, Mutny, and Krause (2020) study coreset methods tailored to neural networks.

Similar questions have also been explored within machine teaching. For instance, Ma et al. (2018) study a setting where a teacher, who knows the target concept, selects a small subdataset from a sample drawn IID from the population to train the learner. This setup is closely related to our problem, with the key difference that the selection process in our setting operates directly on D rather than an intermediate sample. Their analysis focuses on the maximum likelihood estimator for the mean of a Gaussian and the large-margin classifier in one dimension.

Appendix B Proofs

B.1 Carathéodory’s Theorem for Convex Functions

Proposition (Carathéodory’s Theorem for Convex Functions).

Let K⊆ℝdK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be convex and closed, and let f1,…,fn:K→ℝf_{1},\dots,f_{n}:K\to\mathbb{R} be strictly convex functions. Then, for any g∈𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(f1,…,fn)g\in\mathtt{conv}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}), there exist indices i1≤…≤id+1i_{1}\leq\ldots\leq i_{d+1} and a function g′∈𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(fi1,…,fid+1)g^{\prime}\in\mathtt{conv}(f_{i_{1}},\dots,f_{i_{d+1}}) such that:

  1. 1.

    arg⁡minx∈K​g′​(x)=arg⁡minx∈K⁡g⁡(x)\arg\min_{x\in K}g^{\prime}(x)=\arg\min_{x\in K}g(x), and

  2. 2.

    minx∈K⁡g′​(x)≤minx∈K⁡g⁡(x)\min_{x\in K}g^{\prime}(x)\leq\min_{x\in K}g(x).

Before we begin the proof, we recall some basic concepts from convex function analysis. A function f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} is strictly convex if, for all x,y∈ℝdx,y\in\mathbb{R}^{d} with x≠yx\neq y, and for any λ∈(0,1)\lambda\in(0,1), it holds that f⁡(λ​x+(1−λ)​y)<λ​f​(x)+(1−λ)​f​(y).f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)<\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y). This definition is like the definition of convex functions, but with a strict inequality replacing the non-strict one. A key property of strictly convex functions is that they have a unique global minimum, as the strict inequality prevents any other point from achieving the same minimum value. A vector g∈ℝdg\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a subgradient of a convex function f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} at a point ξ∈ℝd\xi\in\mathbb{R}^{d} if:

f⁡(y)≥f⁡(ξ)+⟨g,y−ξ⟩for all ​y∈ℝd.f(y)\geq f(\xi)+\langle g,y-\xi\rangle\quad\text{for all }y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

The set of all subgradients of ff at ξ\xi is called the subdifferential and is denoted ∂f⁡(ξ)\partial f(\xi). The Minkowski sum of two sets A,B⊆ℝdA,B\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} is defined as:

A+B={a+b∣a∈A,b∈B}.A+B=\{a+b\mid a\in A,b\in B\}.

We will use the following fundamental result:

Proposition 12 (Additivity of Subgradients (Rockafellar, 1997, p. 223)).

Let K⊆ℝdK\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be convex and closed, and let f,g:K→ℝf,g:K\to\mathbb{R} be convex functions. For any ξ∈K\xi\in K, it holds that:

∂(f+g)​(ξ)=∂f⁡(ξ)+∂g⁡(ξ).\partial\left(f+g\right)(\xi)=\partial f(\xi)+\partial g(\xi).

This result generalizes the familiar fact that the gradient of a sum is the sum of the gradients, extending it to convex functions that are not necessarily differentiable. We will also use the following simple fact:

Lemma 13.

Let f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be strictly convex. Then 0∈∂f⁡(ξ)0\in\partial f(\xi) if and only if ξ\xi is the unique global minimum of ff.

Proof.

Suppose 0∈∂f⁡(ξ)0\in\partial f(\xi). By the definition of the subgradient:

f⁡(y)≥f⁡(ξ)+⟨0,y−ξ⟩=f⁡(ξ),∀y∈ℝd.f(y)\geq f(\xi)+\langle 0,y-\xi\rangle=f(\xi),\quad\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

Thus, f⁡(ξ)f(\xi) is a global minimum. Since ff is strictly convex, the global minimum is unique, so ξ\xi is the unique minimizer. Conversely, if ξ\xi is the unique global minimum, then f⁡(y)≥f⁡(ξ)f(y)\geq f(\xi) for all y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. By the subgradient definition, 0∈∂f⁡(ξ)0\in\partial f(\xi). This proves the claim. ∎

Proof of Proposition 2.

The proof follows a similar inductive sparsification process for the convex combination as in the classical Carathéodory Theorem (see, e.g. (Matoušek, 2002) page 6 Theorem 1.2.3, originally in  (Carathéodory, 1907)). The key difference is the need for a more careful selection during sparsification to ensure the second item (the inequality between the minimum values) is preserved.

We prove the result by induction on nn, the number of functions in the convex combination. The base case n≤d+1n\leq d+1 is trivial since g′=gg^{\prime}=g satisfies the conclusion. For n>d+1n>d+1, write g∈𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡(f1,…,fn)g\in\mathtt{conv}(f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) as:

g=∑i=1nλi​fi,where ​λi≥0​ and ​∑i=1nλi=1.g=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}f_{i},\quad\text{where }\lambda_{i}\geq 0\text{ and }\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}=1.

Further assume that λi>0\lambda_{i}>0 for all ii; if this is not the case, and λi=0\lambda_{i}=0 for some ii, then we can remove fif_{i} from the convex combination and apply induction. Let ξ=arg⁡minx∈K⁡g⁡(x)\xi=\arg\min_{x\in K}g(x). By Lemma 13, 0∈∂g⁡(ξ)0\in\partial g(\xi), so:

0=∑i=1nλi​yi,with ​yi∈∂fi​(ξ).0=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}y_{i},\quad\text{with }y_{i}\in\partial f_{i}(\xi).

Since n>d+1n>d+1, the vectors {yn−y1,…,yn−yn−1}⊂ℝd\{y_{n}-y_{1},\dots,y_{n}-y_{n-1}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} are linearly dependent. Thus, there exist coefficients β1,…,βn\beta_{1},\dots,\beta_{n} such that ∑i=1nβi​yi=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_{i}y_{i}=0, where ∑i=1nβi=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_{i}=0. Define λi​(t)=λi+t​βi\lambda_{i}(t)=\lambda_{i}+t\beta_{i} and the corresponding functions:

g⁡(x,t)=∑i=1nλi​(t)​fi​(x).g(x,t)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}(t)f_{i}(x).

Notice that ∑i=1nλi​(t)=1\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}(t)=1 for all tt and, since λi​(0)=λi>0\lambda_{i}(0)=\lambda_{i}>0, it follows that for a small enough |t|>0\lvert t\rvert>0, λi​(t)≥0\lambda_{i}(t)\geq 0. Let TT be the maximal interval containing t=0t=0 such that λi​(t)≥0\lambda_{i}(t)\geq 0 for all ii. At least one λi​(t)\lambda_{i}(t) becomes zero at the endpoints t0,t1t_{0},t_{1} of TT. Since for every fixed xx, g⁡(x,t)g(x,t) is linear in tt, its minimum over KK occurs at t0t_{0} or t1t_{1}. Let t∗∈{t0,t1}t^{*}\in\{t_{0},t_{1}\} minimize g⁡(ξ,t)g(\xi,t). At t=t∗t=t^{*}, the corresponding function:

gt⋆​(x)=g⁡(x,t⋆)=∑i=1nλi​(t∗)​fi​(x)g_{t^{\star}}(x)=g(x,t^{\star})=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_{i}(t^{*})f_{i}(x)

involves fewer than nn strictly positive coefficients and satisfies the conditions:

arg⁡minx∈K​gt⋆​(x)=arg⁡minx∈K⁡g⁡(x),minx∈K⁡gt⋆​(x)≤minx∈K⁡g⁡(x).\arg\min_{x\in K}g_{t^{\star}}(x)=\arg\min_{x\in K}g(x),\quad\min_{x\in K}g_{t^{\star}}(x)\leq\min_{x\in K}g(x).

Applying induction on gt⋆g_{t^{\star}} finishes the proof of Proposition. ∎

B.2 Mean Estimation: Proof of Theorem 1

Theorem (Theorem 1 Restatement).

For every n≥1n\geq 1,

supD⊆ℝLD⋆​(n)LD⋆=2​n2​n−1,\sup_{D\subseteq\mathbb{R}}\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(n)}{L_{D}^{\star}}=\frac{2n}{2n-1},

where DD ranges over all finite multisets of ℝ\mathbb{R}. Above, the ratio LD⋆​(n)LD⋆\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(n)}{L^{\star}_{D}} is defined to be 11 when LD⋆​(n)=LD⋆=0L_{D}^{\star}(n)=L_{D}^{\star}=0. If only LD⋆=0L_{D}^{\star}=0, the ratio is defined as ∞\infty.

It is convenient to allow the dataset DD to be any finitely supported distribution, rather than a finite multiset. Importantly, the data-selection process remains unchanged in this formulation: the data selector can choose any sequence of nn points from the support of DD and is evaluated based on the loss incurred by the average of these nn points. This formulation is equivalent to the original problem, as finite multisets correspond to rational distributions, and rational distributions are dense in the set of all finitely supported distributions.

Throughout the proof, we rely on the following lemma, which can be derived through a straightforward calculation:

Lemma 14.

Let DD be a distribution supported on ℝ\mathbb{R}. For any point h∈ℝh\in\mathbb{R}, the squared loss function LD​(h)L_{D}(h) satisfies:

LD​(h)=LD⋆+‖h−μD‖2,L_{D}(h)=L_{D}^{\star}+\|h-\mu_{D}\|^{2},

where μD=𝔼z∼Dz\mu_{D}=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}\displaylimits_{z\sim D}z is the mean of DD.

Lower Bound.

We begin by proving the lower bound using the simple dataset DD consisting of 2​n−12n-1 copies of 00 and a single copy of 11. A direct calculation yields the optimal loss:

LD⋆=2​n−12​n​(12​n−0)2+12​n​(12​n−1)2=2​n−1(2​n)2.L^{\star}_{D}=\frac{2n-1}{2n}\Bigl(\frac{1}{2n}-0\Bigr)^{2}+\frac{1}{2n}\Bigl(\frac{1}{2n}-1\Bigr)^{2}=\frac{2n-1}{(2n)^{2}}.

If we select only nn points from DD, the achievable averages are restricted to the set {0,k/n:k<n}\{0,k/n:k<n\}. Applying Lemma 14, we compute:

LD⋆​(n)LD⋆=LD⋆+(1/2​n)2LD⋆=2​n2​n−1,\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(n)}{L^{\star}_{D}}=\frac{L^{\star}_{D}+(1/2n)^{2}}{L^{\star}_{D}}=\frac{2n}{2n-1},

and hence supD⊆ℝLD⋆​(n)LD⋆≥2​n2​n−1\sup_{D\subseteq\mathbb{R}}\frac{L_{D}^{\star}(n)}{L_{D}^{\star}}\geq\frac{2n}{2n-1}.

Upper Bound.

We now turn to the upper bound, which requires more work. Following the proof outline, we proceed in two steps: (i) use Proposition 2 to reduce the problem to the case where DD consists of only two points, and (ii) explicitly analyze this reduced case.

Step 1: Reduction to two points.

Let DD be a (finitely supported) distribution over ℝ\mathbb{R}. B.3 Classification

B.3.1 Proof of Theorem 4

Theorem (Theorem 4 Restatement).

Let A⋆A^{\star} denote the max-margin algorithm. Then,

supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A⋆)={0if ​n>d,12if ​n≤d,\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})=\begin{cases}0&\text{if }n>d,\\ \frac{1}{2}&\text{if }n\leq d,\end{cases}

where DD ranges over all realizable datasets. Furthermore, A⋆A^{\star} is optimal in the sense that for every continuous ERM AA (and even for any continuous proper learner),

(∀n≤d):supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A)≥12.(\forall n\leq d):\quad\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)\geq\frac{1}{2}.
Proof.

The fact that the max-margin algorithm A⋆A^{\star} satisfies supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A⋆)=0\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})=0 whenever n>dn>d follows from (Vapnik and Chervonenkis, 1974); see also Appendix A of Long and Long (2020). It remains to show that when n≤dn\leq d, supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A⋆)≤12\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})\leq\frac{1}{2} for the max-margin algorithm, and that supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A)≥12\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)\geq\frac{1}{2} for any continuous proper learner AA.

The first part follows from the observation that when presented with only positively labeled examples or only negatively labeled examples, the max-margin algorithm outputs the constant +1+1 or −1-1 hypothesis, respectively. Thus, by selecting a single example from DD whose label matches the majority label, it follows that supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A⋆)≤12.\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})\leq\frac{1}{2}.

We now turn to the more challenging task of proving that for any continuous proper learner AA, we have supD∈𝚁𝚎𝚊𝚕⁡(ℋd)LD⋆​(n,A)≥12\sup_{D\in\mathtt{Real}(\mathcal{H}_{d})}L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)\geq\frac{1}{2} whenever n≤dn\leq d. Let AA be a continuous proper learner and let η>0\eta>0. Using the probabilistic method, we construct a dataset DD such that LD⋆​(n,A)≥12−ηL^{\star}_{D}(n;A)\geq\frac{1}{2}-\eta as follows. We claim that, with probability >0>0, the dataset DD satisfies the following properties:

  2. 2.

Let us begin with the first property. We claim that the first property holds with probability 11. Pr⁡[{(xij,yij)}j=1d​ is not realizable by ​ℋd]\displaystyle\Pr[\{(x_{i_{j}},y_{i_{j}})\}_{j=1}^{d}\text{ is not realizable by }\mathcal{H}_{d}] =Pr[𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟{xij:yij=+1}∩𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟{xij:yij=−1}≠∅]\displaystyle=\Pr\Bigl[\mathtt{conv}\{x_{i_{j}}:y_{i_{j}}=+1\}\cap\mathtt{conv}\{x_{i_{j}}:y_{i_{j}}=-1\}\neq\emptyset\Bigr]

x=∑j:yij=+1αjxij=∑j:yij=−1βjxij,x=\sum_{j:y_{i_{j}}=+1}\alpha_{j}x_{i_{j}}=\sum_{j:y_{i_{j}}=-1}\beta_{j}x_{i_{j}},

We next show that the second property holds with high probability. Specifically, we prove:

B.3.2 Proof of Theorem 5

Theorem (Restatement of Theorem 5).

Every hypothesis class ℋ⊆{±1}X\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{X} satisfies exactly one of the following:

  1. 1.

    𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)=1\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)=1, for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. (Trivial Rate)

  2. 2.

    C1n≤𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)≤C2⋅log⁡nn\frac{C_{1}}{n}\leq\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)\leq\frac{C_{2}\cdot\log n}{n}, for all n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}. Here C1=C1​(ℋ),C2=C2​(ℋ)C_{1}=C_{1}(\mathcal{H}),C_{2}=C_{2}(\mathcal{H}) are positive constants that depend on ℋ\mathcal{H} (but not on nn). (Linear Rate)

  3. 3.

    𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)=0\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)=0, for all sufficiently large n≥n0​(ℋ)n\geq n_{0}(\mathcal{H}). (Zero Rate)

We will rely on basic results from the theory of ε\varepsilon-nets for families with bounded VC dimension and star number. We begin with some useful definitions.

Definition 16 (ε\varepsilon-nets).

Let XX be a set, let ℱ⊆2X\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{X} be a family of subsets of XX, and let PP be a distribution over XX. An ε\varepsilon-net for ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to PP is a set S⊆XS\subseteq X such that for every F∈ℱF\in\mathcal{F},

P⁡(F)>ε⇒F∩S≠∅.P(F)>\varepsilon\quad\Rightarrow\quad F\cap S\neq\emptyset.

In other words, SS intersects every set in ℱ\mathcal{F} that has probability measure greater than ε\varepsilon.

Definition 17 (Star Number for Set Families).

Let XX be a set and let ℱ\mathcal{F} be a family of subsets of XX. The star number of ℱ\mathcal{F} , denoted sℱs_{\mathcal{F}}, is the largest n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that there exist points x1,…,xn∈𝒳x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathcal{X} satisfying

(∀i∈{0,…,n})​(∃Si∈ℱ):Si∩{x1,…,xn}={xi}.(\forall i\in\{0,\dots,n\})(\exists S_{i}\in\mathcal{F}):S_{i}\cap\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\}=\{x_{i}\}.

If no such largest nn exists, define 𝔰ℱ=∞\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{F}}=\infty.

Definition 18 (Star Number for Hypothesis Classes).

Let 𝒳\mathcal{X} be a set and let hypothesis class ℋ⊆{±1}𝒳\mathcal{H}\subseteq\{\pm 1\}^{\mathcal{X}} and let h∈ℋh\in\mathcal{H}. The star number of ℋ\mathcal{H} centered at hh, denoted sh=sh​(ℋ)s_{h}=s_{h}(\mathcal{H}), is the largest n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} such that there exist points x1,…,xn∈𝒳x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in\mathcal{X} satisfying

∀i∈{0,…,n},∃hi∈ℋ​ such that ​∀j∈{1,…,n},hi​(xj)=h⁡(xj)⇔j≠i.\forall i\in\{0,\dots,n\},\ \exists h_{i}\in\mathcal{H}\text{ such that }\forall j\in\{1,\dots,n\},\ h_{i}(x_{j})=h(x_{j})\iff j\neq i.

If no such largest nn exists, define sh=∞s_{h}=\infty. The star number of ℋ\mathcal{H} is defined as 𝔰ℋ=suph∈ℋsh.\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{H}}=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}}s_{h}.

We will rely on the following upper bounds on ε\varepsilon-nets in terms of the VC dimension and star number:

Theorem 19 (ε\varepsilon-nets (Haussler and Welzl, 1987; Hanneke and Yang, 2015)).

Let ℱ⊆2X\mathcal{F}\subseteq 2^{X} be a family of sets. Then,

  1. 1.

    If 𝔰ℱ<∞\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{F}}<\infty then for every distribution PP over XX and every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists an ε\varepsilon-net for ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to PP of size at most 𝔰ℱ\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{F}}.

  2. 2.

    If 𝚟𝚌⁡(ℱ)<∞\mathtt{vc}(\mathcal{F})<\infty then for every distribution PP over XX and every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists an ε\varepsilon-net for ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to PP of size at most O⁡(𝚟𝚌⁡(ℱ)​log⁡(1/ε)ε)O(\frac{\mathtt{vc}(\mathcal{F})\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}), where the big oh conceals a multiplicative universal numerical constant.

To establish Theorem 5, we consider 4 cases:

  1. 1.

    If 𝔰ℋ<∞\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{H}}<\infty, then 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)=0\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)=0 for every n≥𝔰ℋn\geq\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{H}}.

  2. 2.

    If 𝔰ℋ=∞\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{H}}=\infty, we show that 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n) is lower bounded by 1n+1\frac{1}{n+1} for all nn.

  3. 3.

    If the VC dimension of ℋ\mathcal{H} is finite, i.e., 𝚟𝚌⁡(ℋ)=d<∞\mathtt{vc}(\mathcal{H})=d<\infty then 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)≤O⁡(d​log⁡nn)\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)\leq O(\frac{d\log n}{n}) for all nn.

  4. 4.

    If 𝚟𝚌⁡(ℋ)=∞\mathtt{vc}(\mathcal{H})=\infty, we prove that 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)=1\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)=1 for all nn.

These statements together establish the proof of Theorem 5.

Case 1: 𝔰⁡(ℋ)<∞\mathfrak{s}(\mathcal{H})<\infty.

Given a dataset DD, consider a maximal realizable subdataset D′⊆DD^{\prime}\subseteq D. Noting that the optimal loss on DD satisfies

LD⋆=minh∈ℋ⁡LD​(h)=|D|−|D′||D|.L^{\star}_{D}=\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}L_{D}(h)=\frac{\lvert D\rvert-\lvert D^{\prime}\rvert}{\lvert D\rvert}.

Consider the following family of datasets:

err⁡(ℋ∣D′)={err⁡(h∣D′):h∈ℋ},\operatorname{err}(\mathcal{H}\mid D^{\prime})=\bigl\{\operatorname{err}(h\mid D^{\prime}):h\in\mathcal{H}\bigr\},

where err⁡(h∣D′)={(x,y)∈D′:h⁡(x)≠y}\operatorname{err}(h\mid D^{\prime})=\{(x,y)\in D^{\prime}:h(x)\neq y\} is the subdataset of D′D^{\prime} which hh classifies incorrectly. Notice that the star number of err⁡(ℋ∣D′)\operatorname{err}(\mathcal{H}\mid D^{\prime}) is at most 𝔰ℋ\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{H}}. Let PP be the uniform distribution over D′D^{\prime}. By Theorem 19, for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists an ε\varepsilon-net Dε′⊆D′D^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\subseteq D^{\prime} for err⁡(ℋ∣D′)\operatorname{err}(\mathcal{H}\mid D^{\prime}) with respect to PP of size at most 𝔰ℋ\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{H}}. Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an ERM for ℋ\mathcal{H} and let h=𝒜⁡(Dε′)h=\mathcal{A}(D^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}) denote the output hypothesis of 𝒜\mathcal{A} when given the ε\varepsilon-net as input. Thus, by the ε\varepsilon-net property it follows that LD′​(h)≤εL_{D^{\prime}}(h)\leq\varepsilon. Consequently, the total error on the full dataset DD is bounded by LD⋆+ε.L^{\star}_{D}+\varepsilon. Since this holds for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, we obtain 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n,A)<ε\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n,A)<\varepsilon, implying that 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n,A)=0\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n,A)=0, thus establishing the claim.

Case 2: 𝔰ℋ=∞\mathfrak{s}_{\mathcal{H}}=\infty.

Given nn, select a dataset DD that forms the center of a star-set of size n+1n+1. Such a dataset is realizable. Now, consider an ERM that, whenever possible, avoids selecting the center hypothesis—specifically, when presented with any proper subdataset of DD, it chooses a hypothesis that is inconsistent with at least one point in DD. Consequently, that learner will misclassify at least one of the n+1n+1 points, leading to an error rate of at least 1n+1\frac{1}{n+1}. This establishes the desired lower bound:

𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)≥1n+1.\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)\geq\frac{1}{n+1}.
Case 3: 𝚟𝚌⁡(ℋ)=d<∞\mathtt{vc}(\mathcal{H})=d<\infty.

The argument here is identical to the argument in Case 1. The only difference is that we invoke the 2nd Item of Theorem 19 which applies to the VC dimension. Specifically, given a selection budget of nn points, we obtain an ε⁡(n)\varepsilon(n)-net Dε′⊆D′D^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\subseteq D^{\prime} for

ε⁡(n)=O⁡(d​log⁡(n/d)n+log⁡(1/δ)n).\varepsilon(n)=O\left(\frac{d\log(n/d)}{n}+\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}\right).

such that applying any ERM on Dε′⊆D′D^{\prime}_{\varepsilon}\subseteq D^{\prime} yields an hypothesis whose loss is at most LD⋆+ε⁡(n)L^{\star}_{D}+\varepsilon(n).

Using this bound, we obtain an upper bound of the form 𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)=O⁡(d​log⁡nn)\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)=O(\frac{d\log n}{n}), establishing the linear rate.

Case 4: 𝚟𝚌⁡(ℋ)=∞\mathtt{vc}(\mathcal{H})=\infty.

Following a similar approach to the 𝔰⁡(ℋ)=∞\mathfrak{s}(\mathcal{H})=\infty case, we now leverage the fact that ℋ\mathcal{H} has infinite VC dimension. Specifically, for any given nn and arbitrarily small ε>0\varepsilon>0, we select a shattered set of size N=n/εN=n/\varepsilon. Next, construct a dataset DD on this shattered set in which all points are labeled +1+1. Consider a learner that, for any point in DD not included in its training subset, always predicts −1-1. Since the dataset is shattered, there exists a hypothesis in ℋ\mathcal{H} consistent with any labeling of DD, meaning the learner’s choice is valid within the hypothesis class. By construction, the learner correctly classifies only the nn training points, while misclassifying the remaining N−nN-n points. This results in an error rate of N−nN=1−nN=1−ε.\frac{N-n}{N}=1-\frac{n}{N}=1-\varepsilon. Taking the limit as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0 yields a lower bound of 11, establishing the claim:

𝚁ℋ⋆​(n)≥1.\mathtt{R}_{\mathcal{H}}^{\star}(n)\geq 1.

B.4 Stochastic Convex Optimization

B.4.1 Proof of Theorem 9

Theorem (Theorem 9 Restatement).

Let A⋆A^{\star} denote the min-norm ERM. Then,

supDLD⋆​(n,A)LD⋆={1if ​n≥2​d,d+1if ​n=d,∞if ​n<d,\sup_{D}\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)}{L^{\star}_{D}}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }n{\geq 2d},\\ d+1&\text{if }n=d,\\ \infty&\text{if }n<d,\end{cases}

where DD ranges over all finite datasets and LD⋆=infw∈𝒲LD​(w)L^{\star}_{D}=\inf_{w\in\mathcal{W}}L_{D}(w) denotes the optimal population loss. Above, the ratio LD⋆​(n,A)LD⋆\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(n;A)}{L^{\star}_{D}} is defined to be 11 when both the numerator and denominator are 00. If only the denominator is 00, the ratio is defined as ∞\infty.

Furthermore, the lower bound in the cased n<dn<d holds for every weakly continuous ERM.

The proof proceeds in two steps: we first derive an upper bound for each of the three cases—n≥2​dn\geq 2d, n=dn=d, and n<dn<d—and establish show the corresponding lower bounds.

Remark 20.

Without loss of generality, we restrict our analysis to datasets DD whose feature vectors {x∣(x,y)∈D}\{x\mid(x,y)\in D\} span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Indeed, if the feature vectors lie in a lower-dimensional subspace, we can analyze the problem within that subspace instead. This does not compromise generality, since for any w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, we have LD​(w)=LD​(w|⁣|)L_{D}(w)=L_{D}(w_{||}), where w|⁣|w_{||} is the projection of ww onto the space spanned by the feature vectors (see Lemma 21).

Upper Bounds

Case 1: n≥2​dn\geq 2d

Had the loss functions in linear regression been strictly convex, we could have directly applied Proposition 2, yielding a stronger result with a selection budget of d+1d+1 rather than 2​d2d. However, since the loss functions are not strictly convex and the empirical risk minimizer is not unique, additional care is required to handle this case.

In linear regression, the loss function for an example z=(x,y)z=(x,y) is given by

ℓz​(w)=(w⋅x−y)2,\ell_{z}(w)=(w\cdot x-y)^{2},

where w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. While this function is convex in ww, it is not strictly convex for d>1d>1 and has multiple empirical risk minimizers. Among them, the min-norm ERM A⋆A^{\star} selects the solution w⋆w^{\star} with the smallest Euclidean norm. A key property of this solution is that it always lies within the span of the input vectors {xi∣(xi,yi)∈D}\{x_{i}\mid(x_{i},y_{i})\in D\}. This is formalized in the following lemma:

Lemma 21.

Let D={(xi,yi)}i=1ND=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}. The min-norm minimizer of LD​(⋅)L_{D}(\cdot) is unique and it belongs to span({xi∣i=1,…,N}).\mathrm{span}\bigl(\{x_{i}\mid i=1,\ldots,N\}\bigr). Moreover, any minimizer of LD​(⋅)L_{D}(\cdot) can be expressed as w|⁣|+w⟂w_{||}+w_{\perp}, where w⟂⟂span({xi∣i=1,…,N}),w_{\perp}\perp\mathrm{span}\bigl(\{x_{i}\mid i=1,\ldots,N\}\bigr), and w|⁣|w_{||} is the projection of ww on span({xi∣i=1,…,N})\mathrm{span}\bigl(\{x_{i}\mid i=1,\ldots,N\}\bigr).

Proof.

The proof follows from basic linear algebra: any vector ww can be decomposed as w=w|⁣|+w⟂w=w_{||}+w_{\perp}, where w|⁣|w_{||} lies in the span of {xi∣i=1,…,N}\{x_{i}\mid i=1,\ldots,N\} and w⟂w_{\perp} is orthogonal to it. Since only the component within the span contributes to the loss LD​(w)L_{D}(w), both ww and w|⁣|w_{||} achieve the same loss. However, w|⁣|w_{||} has a strictly smaller Euclidean norm, implying that the min-norm loss minimizer must lie within the span. Furthermore, any other loss minimizer can differ from ww only by a component orthogonal to the span, completing the proof. ∎

By Lemma 21, it suffices to find a dataset of nn examples D′={(xij,yij)}j=1nD^{\prime}=\{(x_{i_{j}},y_{i_{j}})\}_{j=1}^{n} such that w⋆w^{\star} minimizes LD′​(⋅)L_{D^{\prime}}(\cdot) and

w⋆∈span({xij∣j=1,…,n}).w^{\star}\in\mathrm{span}\bigl(\{x_{i_{j}}\mid j=1,\ldots,n\}\bigr).

We establish this using an argument similar to the one in the proof of Proposition 2, namely, by applying Carathéodory’s theorem to the gradients. A naive application of Carathéodory’s theorem, as in the proof of Proposition 2, guarantees the existence of a weighted subdataset of size d+1d+1 for which w⋆w^{\star} minimizes the corresponding weighted loss function. However, the issue is that other minimizers may exist, and some may have smaller norm then w⋆w^{\star}. To ensure uniqueness, we show that selecting 2​d2d points instead of d+1d+1 suffices. Moreover, this increase in the selection budget is necessary, as demonstrated in Example 23.

By Remark 20, we may assume that span⁡({xi∣(xi,yi)∈D})=ℝd\mathrm{span}(\{x_{i}\mid(x_{i},y_{i})\in D\})=\mathbb{R}^{d}, and hence the minimizer of LD​(⋅)L_{D}(\cdot) is unique and equals to w⋆w^{\star}. Since the function LD​(⋅)L_{D}(\cdot) is differentiable, we have 0=∇LD​(w⋆)0=\nabla L_{D}(w^{\star}), where ∇LD​(w⋆)\nabla L_{D}(w^{\star}) denotes the gradient of LD​(⋅)L_{D}(\cdot) at w⋆w^{\star}. By linearity,

0=∑i=1N1N∇ℓzi(w⋆).0=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{N}\nabla\ell_{z_{i}}(w^{\star}).

Observe that for z=(x,y)z=(x,y) the gradient of ℓz​(⋅)\ell_{z}(\cdot) is parallel to xx, specifically: ∇ℓz​(w)=c⋅x\nabla\ell_{z}(w)=c\cdot x, where cc is the scalar c=2​sign⁡(w​x−y)​|ℓz​(w)|c=2\operatorname{sign}(wx-y)\sqrt{\lvert\ell_{z}(w)\rvert}. We split the proof into two cases. First, we assume that {∇ℓzi​(w⋆)}\{\nabla\ell_{z_{i}}(w^{\star})\} spans ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and proceed with the proof under this assumption. Later, we will address the complementary case where {∇ℓzi​(w⋆)}\{\nabla\ell_{z_{i}}(w^{\star})\} does not span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and explain how to handle it.

In the first case, 00 is an interior point of 𝚌𝚘𝚗𝚟⁡({∇ℓzi​(w⋆):1≤i≤N})\mathtt{conv}(\{\nabla\ell_{z_{i}}(w^{\star}):1\leq i\leq N\}), because it is average of all points ∇ℓzi​(w⋆)\nabla\ell_{z_{i}}(w^{\star}) and they span the ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. We proceed by employing a variant of Carathéodory’s theorem, due to Steinitz (Matoušek et al., 2003, p. 8), originally from Steinitz (1916).

Theorem (Steinitz (1916)).

Consider X⊂ℝdX\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and xx a point in the interior of the convex hull of XX. Then, xx belongs to the interior of the convex hull of a set of at most 2​d2d points of XX.

By applying Steinitz’s theorem, we can find a subdataset D′D^{\prime} for which the corresponding gradients {∇ℓzij​(w⋆)}\{\nabla\ell_{z_{i_{j}}}(w^{\star})\} still contain 00 as a dd-interior point of their convex hull. In particular D′D^{\prime} must be full dimensional (i.e. its feature vectors span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}) and hence, by Lemma 21, w⋆w^{\star} remains the unique minimizer for this subdataset (since the feature vectors of the subdataset span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}). Thus, this subdataset achieves the desired bound.

In the second case, suppose that {∇ℓzi​(w⋆)}\{\nabla\ell_{z_{i}}(w^{\star})\} does not span ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, and let VV be the subspace it spans. Consider the subdataset consisting of points whose loss has a non-zero gradient on w⋆w^{\star} {zij∣ℓzij​(w⋆)≠0}\{z_{i_{j}}\mid\ell_{z_{i_{j}}}(w^{\star})\neq 0\}. The function w⋆w^{\star} remains an ERM on this subdataset, but it is not necessarily the min-norm ERM. Let w′⁣⋆w^{\prime\star} denote the min-norm ERM computed on this subdataset. Since VV has dimension d′<dd^{\prime}<d, the first part of the proof guarantees the existence of a weighted dataset of 2​d′2d^{\prime} points whose feature vectors span VV and for which the min-norm ERM outputs w′⁣⋆w^{\prime\star}, while Lemma 21 guarantees that w⋆w^{\star} is also an ERM for this weighted dataset. We augment this set by adding d−d′d-d^{\prime} points for which ℓz​(w⋆)=0\ell_{z}(w^{\star})=0, ensuring that the full set of d+d′d+d^{\prime} points spans ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. Since adding realizable points does not affect the gradient value at w⋆w^{\star}, it remains an ERM for this augmented dataset. By Lemma 21, w⋆w^{\star} is now the unique minimizer, implying that it is also the minimum-norm solution.

Case 2: 𝒏=𝒅\boldsymbol{n=d}.

We now show that for any dataset DD in ℝd×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} with n=dn=d examples, the ratio supDLD⋆​(d,A)LD⋆\sup_{D}\frac{L^{\star}_{D}(d;A)}{L^{\star}_{D}} is at most d+1d+1. The result follows directly from Theorem 5 of Derezinski and Warmuth (2017):

Theorem (Theorem 5, Derezinski and Warmuth (2017)).

If the input matrix 𝐗∈ℝd×n\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} is in general position, then for any label vector 𝐲∈ℝn\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, the expected squared loss (over all nn labeled vectors) of the optimal solution 𝐰∗​(S)\mathbf{w}^{*}(S) for the subproblem (𝐗S,𝐲S)(\mathbf{X}_{S},\mathbf{y}_{S}), where the dd-element subset SS is obtained via volume sampling, satisfies:

𝔼⁡[L⁡(𝐰∗​(S))]=(d+1)​L​(𝐰∗).\mathbb{E}[L(\mathbf{w}^{*}(S))]=(d+1)L(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

If 𝐗\mathbf{X} is not in general position, the expected loss is upper-bounded by (d+1)​L​(𝐰∗)(d+1)L(\mathbf{w}^{*}).

Above, the subproblem (XS,yS)(X_{S},y_{S}) corresponds to applying an ERM on the subdataset SS. Volume sampling refers to selecting SS from a distribution over all subdatasets of DD of size n=dn=d. Specifically, each subdataset SS is sampled with probability proportional to the volume of the parallelogram spanned by the feature vectors {x:(x,y)∈S}\{x:(x,y)\in S\}. As a result, only subdatasets SS whose feature vectors form a basis of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} are sampled. This ensures that every ERM applied to SS returns the unique hypothesis that interpolates the data. Overall, this establishes, via a probabilistic argument, that there exists a subdataset SS of size n=dn=d such that any ERM applied to it returns a hypothesis whose loss is at most d+1d+1 times the optimal solution LD⋆L_{D}^{\star}.

For n<dn<d, we only need to prove a lower bound.

B.4.2 Analysis of Examples for Theorem 11

Example 22 (Strict Convexity Requirement).

We provide a 22-dimensional construction, which can be extended to higher dimensions.

For a vector v∈ℝdv\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, define fv:ℝd→ℝf_{v}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} by

fv​(x)={0,if ​|⟨v,x⟩|≤1,|⟨v,x⟩|−1,otherwise,f_{v}(x)=\begin{cases}0,&\text{if }|\langle v,x\rangle|\leq 1,\\ |\langle v,x\rangle|-1,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}

where ⟨v,x⟩\langle v,x\rangle is the scalar product of vv and xx. Note that fvf_{v} is convex but not strictly convex.

Let v1,v2,v3∈ℝ2v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} be such that the triangle v1​v2​v3v_{1}v_{2}v_{3} is regular, and consider the dataset D={fv1,fv2,fv3}D=\{f_{v_{1}},f_{v_{2}},f_{v_{3}}\} and the function f=fv1+fv2+fv33f=\frac{f_{v_{1}}+f_{v_{2}}+f_{v_{3}}}{3}. The function ff achieves its global minimum with value 00, and the set of global minimizers forms a regular hexagon. Example 23 (Necessity of the n>dn>d Assumption).

We construct an example illustrating that when n≤dn\leq d, the empirical loss LD⋆​(n,A⋆)L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star}) can significantly exceed the population loss LD⋆L^{\star}_{D}.

Consider a set of d+1d+1 points {v1,…,vd+1}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{d+1}\} in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} arranged as a regular simplex, with each point positioned at a distance of 11 from the hyperplane spanned by the remaining dd points. For each vertex viv_{i}, define the loss function as

fvi​(w)=‖w−vi‖P,f_{v_{i}}(w)=\|w-v_{i}\|^{P},

where P>2P>2.

In this case, the minimizer ww must lie within the hyperplane spanned by the remaining dd points: indeed, if ww had a nonzero orthogonal component, say w=w|⁣|+w⟂w=w_{||}+w_{\perp} (where w|⁣|w_{||} lies in the hyperplane and w⟂w_{\perp} is the orthogonal component), then by the Pythagorean theorem, the loss of w|⁣|w_{||} would be strictly smaller than that of ww.

LD⋆​(n,A⋆)≥1d+1.L^{\star}_{D}(n;A^{\star})\geq\frac{1}{d+1}.

Appendix C Continuous ERMs for Linear Regression

Definition 24.

For r≤dr\leq d let Cr⊆(ℝd×ℝ)nC_{r}\subseteq(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R})^{n} denote the set of all datasets (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)∈ℝd×ℝ(x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(x_{n},y_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} such that 𝚍𝚒𝚖⁡(𝚜𝚙𝚊𝚗⁡({xi}i=1n))=r\mathtt{dim}(\mathtt{span}(\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}))=r. An ERM AA is strongly continuous if for every r≤dr\leq d the map which takes a dataset (x1,y1),…,(xn,yn)∈Cr(x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,(x_{n},y_{n})\in C_{r} to the parameters of A⁡((x1,y1),…,xn,yn)A((x_{1},y_{1}),\ldots,x_{n},y_{n}) is continuous on CrC_{r}.

The following result formalizes the sense in which strong continuity is the strongest form of continuity that an ERM can satisfy. Since this result is somewhat tangential to the main focus of this paper, its proof will be provided in the full journal version of this manuscript.

Theorem 25.

There exists a strongly continuous ERM. In particular, any ERM that outputs w∈ℝdw\in\mathbb{R}^{d} that minimizes a strictly convex continuous function R:ℝd→ℝR:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} subject to minimizing the empirical loss is strongly continuous.

This is the strongest form of continuity in the following sense: for every ERM AA and for every r′<r′′≤dr^{\prime}<r^{\prime\prime}\leq d there exists a sequence of datasets {Dm}m=1∞⊆Cr′′\{D_{m}\}_{m=1}^{\infty}\subseteq C_{r^{\prime\prime}} such that limm→∞Dm=D∈Cr′\lim_{m\to\infty}D_{m}=D\in C_{r^{\prime}}, however limm→∞A⁡(Dm)≠A⁡(D)\lim_{m\to\infty}A(D_{m})\neq A(D).
